tagline.text: The Philippines' largest marine protected area, home to wild dolphins between Cebu and Negros

location.label: Location
location.text: Strait between Cebu Island and Negros Island (Cebu's west coast and Negros's east coast)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500~3,000 (per person, Bais dolphin-watching group tour)

children.text: The Tañon Strait Protected Seascape is the Philippines' largest marine protected area, stretching along the strait between Cebu and Negros. Wild dolphins, whales and rich coral make it the backdrop for dolphin watching in Bais and sea trips in Moalboal.
Tañon Strait is a long, narrow stretch of sea separating Cebu and Negros. It is about
160km
long and about
5km
wide at its narrowest in the south, widening to about
27km
, and its deepest point reaches about
. It connects the Visayan Sea to the north with the Bohol Sea to the south. The whole strait was declared a protected seascape in 1998 under
Presidential Proclamation No. 1234
, and its area is given as about
534,589 hectares
. It is widely described as the largest marine protected area in the Philippines.

What makes it special is the number of cetaceans that gather here. About 14 species of whales and dolphins are reported in the strait, and international marine mammal habitat data say that eight species were confirmed in recent surveys. Typical residents include the small, resident Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin, spinner dolphins that come in to rest during the day, and dwarf sperm whales. The strait is also described as home to about 62 percent of the Philippines' coral species, so it is rich in coral, and it is a fishing ground for dozens of towns and cities on both the Cebu and Negros sides.

That said, this is not a park you enter with a ticket; the entire expanse of sea is the protected area. What travelers actually experience are boat tours from Bais Bay to look for dolphins, a visit to the Manjuyod sandbar, the clear waters off Moalboal on Cebu's west coast, and the fishing-village scenery along the shore. Please read this guide as a way to understand the strait as a whole and decide where and how to experience it. On the Cebu side, west-coast towns such as Toledo and Moalboal are key bases, and on the Negros side San Carlos, Bais and Dumaguete are the main towns facing the strait. At the northern end, the Don Islands, including Bantayan, shelter the sea, so on a map the strait looks like one long channel.

The strait is also famous in Philippine environmental legal history. In 2015 the Supreme Court ruled that an oil exploration contract inside the strait (Service Contract No. 46) violated the Constitution and the protected areas law, and declared it void. The case is also known for having listed marine life as petitioners in the name of the protected seascape, so there is plenty to talk about for anyone interested in the environment and travel. The protected area is run by the Protected Area Management Board (PAMB), and at its first general assembly in February 2015 the 2015–2025 General Management Plan was approved. The strait is also described as the first sea area to require vessels docking or transiting to carry vessel monitoring systems, and community sea guards (Bantay Dagat) made up of local residents help enforce rules against illegal commercial fishing. Illegal fishing is still counted among the biggest problems facing this sea.

blocks.title: The Philippines' largest marine protected area

children.text: This is a protected seascape of about
534,589 hectares
declared under Proclamation No. 1234 in 1998. It runs long along the west coast of Cebu Island and the east coast of Negros Island, and the entire strait is protected.

North Bais Bay, off Bais City in Negros Oriental, is famous for dolphin watching. You head out by boat from Canibol wharf in the early morning to look for wild dolphins. How much you see depends on the weather and waves.

This is a stop often combined with the dolphin-watching tour. At low tide you can walk on the exposed sandbar, and at high tide the huts on it look as if they are floating on the water. Check the tides in advance.

blocks.title: Many kinds of whales and dolphins

children.text: About 14 species of cetaceans have been reported in the strait, with spinner dolphins and Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins the best known. Surveys have photo-identified more than 100 bottlenose dolphins alone. The same source says an estimated 3,500 spinner dolphins live here and come into the strait to rest during the day. That is why quiet watching from a respectful distance matters if you want to see dolphins.

A large share of the Philippines' coral species is said to live in this strait. At places like Moalboal on Cebu's west coast you can see the clear waters of the strait up close by snorkeling and diving.
Even at its narrowest in the south, only about
5km
wide, the strait is deep. Deep water and a narrow channel create a unique environment that draws food and large animals.

In 2015 the Supreme Court voided an oil exploration contract inside the strait, making it a landmark case in Philippine environmental law. Local groups and sea guards continue to work to protect this sea.

You arrive at Canibol wharf in Bais and board the boat.
You head out into Bais Bay to look for dolphins. Early morning is said to give a better chance of sightings.
You move on to Manjuyod White Sandbar to stroll on the sandbar and take photos.
You have a seafood lunch on board. Whether it is included in the price differs by tour, so check when booking.
You return to the wharf.
You return to Dumaguete and wrap up at your hotel.

You look at coral and tropical fish in the clear water.

You explore a nearby waterfall or coastal village.
The easiest way to experience the strait from the Cebu side is to use Moalboal as your base. See the Moalboal destination guide as well.
There are several direct flights every day from Manila (NAIA) to Cebu (Mactan-Cebu International Airport, CEB), and the flight takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
. To reach Bais on the Negros side there are also flights to Dumaguete (DGT), so check the latest schedules.
From Cebu airport toward Moalboal (Cebu's west coast) you travel by car or bus, and the travel time varies a lot with traffic, so check locally.
Routes and schedules change often, so check airline notices before booking.
Bais City is about
45km
from Dumaguete, the capital of Negros Oriental.
Tour operators generally pick you up at your Dumaguete hotel and take you to Canibol wharf. You can also go by public transport (bus or van), so check locally.
There are port towns between Cebu and Negros (Toledo on Cebu; San Carlos and Bais on Negros) where you can cross by boat.
Ferry routes and schedules vary by season, so check with the operator or the port before you leave.

Dolphin watching and boat tours are best when the sea is calm. Tour operators generally recommend March to October as the best period, and say that in the winter months, when the northeast monsoon blows, rough waves can make sailing difficult.
Early morning is the best time of day. Many local tour reviews also say it is best to head out before about 9–10 AM.

Your base on the Negros side of the strait is Dumaguete. It has plenty of hotels and restaurants, and many operators offer pickup for Bais tours, so it is a comfortable place to stay. There is lodging in Bais itself, but Dumaguete offers a far wider choice.

Your base on the Cebu side is Moalboal. Dive shops and beach lodging are concentrated there, making it a good place to enjoy the strait's sea up close. Meals center on seafood from the coastal villages, and many Bais tours serve a seafood lunch on board. Many towns on both sides of the strait live off fishing, so you can enjoy fresh grilled fish and seafood dishes at relatively low prices. Lodging tends to fill up early on weekends in the dry high season, so it is safer to book ahead.
Dolphins are wild animals and are not seen every time. Set out early and pick a day with good weather.
Tours start early, so confirm the pickup time at your hotel the day before and get to bed early.
Bring a towel, a change of clothes, slippers or aqua shoes, sunscreen and cash. Souvenir shops on the sandbar often take cash only.
You can walk on the Manjuyod sandbar at low tide, and it is submerged at high tide. Plan your schedule with a tide chart.
When choosing an operator, compare what is included (lunch, fees, pickup) and the cancellation policy. Some offer free cancellation up to 48 hours before.
Choose a responsible operator that does not get too close to dolphins or chase them. Boats surrounding dolphins is not good.

The best protection a traveler can offer is choosing a responsible operator. Before booking, ask whether they keep their distance from dolphins and limit the number of boats. The strait is also where fishers make their living, so do not touch nets or fishing gear, and support local shops and restaurants.
If you get seasick, take medicine beforehand. Even inside the strait, waves rise when the wind picks up.
If the sea is rough, tours can be cancelled, and sighting dolphins is not guaranteed. Do not push on in high waves.
Because this is a protected area, do not step on or touch coral, and do not touch or feed dolphins or whales.
Take your trash back with you and reduce single-use plastic.
In the winter months when the northeast monsoon blows, the sea is rough and plans can change.
Always wear a life vest, and check that the boat is not over capacity.
Rules and prices change often, so check the latest local notices.
